item.title: Assessing the Quality of OSM 3D Building Data Using 3D Geometric Comparison and Machine Learning
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT OpenStreetMap (OSM) is a well‐known platform for Volunteered Geographic Information. Most studies on OSM 3D building quality focus on a single aspect, such as footprint shape errors or attribute completeness. Current machine learning approaches typically analyze 2D footprints, with little attention paid to 3D characteristics like roof geometry or building height. To fill this gap, we propose an integrated framework that combines geometric comparative evaluation with machine‐learning prediction. In this framework, based on footprint Intersection over Union (IoU) and centroid distance, OSM buildings are matched with authoritative or externally validated 3D reference datasets selected for each study area, for example, from national mapping agencies. For the matched OSM buildings, the spatial accuracy is evaluated using location error, height error, building area error, and 3D Hausdorff distance error. For the unmatched buildings, machine learning models are used to predict their quality. We validated the proposed framework in six study areas across Asia and Europe: Beijing, Ningbo, Osaka, Yokohama, Amsterdam, and Almere. In total, the evaluation covers more than 115,000 OSM buildings. Compared with traditional methods, the proposed framework significantly improves facade error detection, evaluation completeness, and the granularity of quality classification, offering new insights for assessing and improving OSM data quality. The results produced in this study are available at: https://github.com/Longtao2002/OSM‐3D‐Building‐Quality‐Assessment.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

OpenStreetMap (OSM) is a well-known platform for Volunteered Geographic Information. Most studies on OSM 3D building quality focus on a single aspect, such as footprint shape errors or attribute completeness. Current machine learning approaches typically analyze 2D footprints, with little attention paid to 3D characteristics like roof geometry or building height. To fill this gap, we propose an integrated framework that combines geometric comparative evaluation with machine-learning prediction. In this framework, based on footprint Intersection over Union (IoU) and centroid distance, OSM buildings are matched with authoritative or externally validated 3D reference datasets selected for each study area, for example, from national mapping agencies. For the matched OSM buildings, the spatial accuracy is evaluated using location error, height error, building area error, and 3D Hausdorff distance error. For the unmatched buildings, machine learning models are used to predict their quality. We validated the proposed framework in six study areas across Asia and Europe: Beijing, Ningbo, Osaka, Yokohama, Amsterdam, and Almere. In total, the evaluation covers more than 115,000 OSM buildings. Compared with traditional methods, the proposed framework significantly improves facade error detection, evaluation completeness, and the granularity of quality classification, offering new insights for assessing and improving OSM data quality. The results produced in this study are available at: https://github.com/Longtao2002/OSM-3D-Building-Quality-Assessment.

item.title: DaiLLM: An Agent Framework Based on a Large Language Model and Reinforced by AI to Generate Daily Activity Trajectories
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Simulating human mobility is crucial for urban planning, environmental exposure assessment, and social behavior studies. However, existing methods often rely on rules and assumptions, making it difficult to provide robust results and explicit decision‐making processes when generating plausible daily activity trajectories from sparse location records such as check‐ins. To bridge these gaps, we propose a large language model (LLM)‐based agent framework that innovatively incorporates the Chain‐of‐Thought (CoT) approach and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) mechanisms, namely Daily mobility LLM (DaiLLM). This framework consists of three modules: the Profiler derives user characteristics from historical trajectory data; the Generator simulates movement through the CoT process, which integrates constraints from Profiler outputs; and the Discriminator employs RLAIF to evaluate the similarity between generated results and real data, providing feedback to optimize the results. Experiments demonstrate that: (1) our method improves accuracy by 34.2% compared to traditional approaches in daily activity trajectory generation; (2) the CoT approach enhances activity logic and results in a 26.1% increase through task decomposition and constraint integration; (3) the RLAIF mechanism explicitly provides an optimization process through Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) analysis; and (4) our method excels in transfer learning and long‐term generation across different city contexts. This study provides a robust, transparent, and cost‐effective solution for plausible daily activity trajectory generation from sparse check‐in data, which will establish a new paradigm for mobility behavior analysis in data‐scarce scenarios.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

Simulating human mobility is crucial for urban planning, environmental exposure assessment, and social behavior studies. However, existing methods often rely on rules and assumptions, making it difficult to provide robust results and explicit decision-making processes when generating plausible daily activity trajectories from sparse location records such as check-ins. To bridge these gaps, we propose a large language model (LLM)-based agent framework that innovatively incorporates the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) approach and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) mechanisms, namely Daily mobility LLM (DaiLLM). This framework consists of three modules: the Profiler derives user characteristics from historical trajectory data; the Generator simulates movement through the CoT process, which integrates constraints from Profiler outputs; and the Discriminator employs RLAIF to evaluate the similarity between generated results and real data, providing feedback to optimize the results. Experiments demonstrate that: (1) our method improves accuracy by 34.2% compared to traditional approaches in daily activity trajectory generation; (2) the CoT approach enhances activity logic and results in a 26.1% increase through task decomposition and constraint integration; (3) the RLAIF mechanism explicitly provides an optimization process through Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) analysis; and (4) our method excels in transfer learning and long-term generation across different city contexts. This study provides a robust, transparent, and cost-effective solution for plausible daily activity trajectory generation from sparse check-in data, which will establish a new paradigm for mobility behavior analysis in data-scarce scenarios.
